solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Like the atlas I found in inaccurate copy — sent back

indicators.note: sending something back returns it the way it came, so the assembled string is read from the end
something found in another sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: lax means careless, not precise
taken as written
to ape is to copy or mimic

explanation.surface: A road atlas full of mistakes has been returned to its publisher.
explanation.walkthrough: The atlas is not a book but the topmost vertebra of the neck; EPAXIAL means lying above the axis, the vertebra on which the atlas turns.
explanation.definitionFit: Anatomically the atlas vertebra sits above the axis vertebra, which is exactly the position the adjective describes.

clue.text: Gives form to executive in triplicate. Is "Expenses" unfilled?

parts.note: an abbreviation for executive
ternal means threefold, in threes
taken as written

indicators.note: a word left unfilled has lost its contents, keeping only its shell of first and last letters

parts.note: only the first and last letters of the word survive

explanation.surface: An office worker filling out forms in triplicate wonders whether the expenses box was left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: TERNAL is a rare Chambers word for threefold, the kind of vocabulary a Mephisto expects; the question mark and quotation marks make 'Expenses' look like a form field rather than fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To externalise something is to give an inner idea outward, concrete shape, which is giving it form.

clue.text: Fog round all the way beside quiet local rivers

parts.note: p, piano, is the musical mark for quiet
ea is a dialect word for a river or stream
a round shape is an O
up can mean completely, as in eat it up

explanation.surface: Fog spreads right round the countryside beside the quiet local rivers.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is written back to front: the round-plus-all-the-way pair comes last in the answer, set beside the quiet-rivers pair.
explanation.definitionFit: Pea soup is the informal name for a thick yellowish fog, likened to the colour and density of the soup.

clue.text: Nomogram's not serviceable form of calculator

parts.note: an abac is a nomogram, a chart for reading off calculations
U/S is the abbreviation for unserviceable

explanation.surface: A nomogram is useless as a kind of calculator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not serviceable' looks like a comment on the nomogram, but it is the abbreviation U/S; the apostrophe-s just joins the two parts.
explanation.definitionFit: An abacus is a frame of sliding beads used for arithmetic, an early kind of calculating device.

clue.text: Fear of the foreign phone box being out of order, taking yen

indicators.note: something out of order is jumbled from its proper sequence, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
Y is the symbol for the Japanese yen

explanation.surface: A tourist abroad finds the phone box broken and swallowing their yen, and starts to fear foreign places.
explanation.definitionFit: Xenophoby is a variant of xenophobia, a dread or dislike of strangers and anything foreign.

clue.text: Excessive post inside American country

indicators.note: one thing placed inside another is surrounded by it, so that piece sits within the outer pair

parts.note: A is a standard abbreviation for American
a bitt is a post on a ship's deck for fastening cables
hick as an adjective means rustic, provincial

explanation.surface: Too much mail is piling up inside some American country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Post' and 'country' read as mail and a nation; they are a deck bollard and a word for rustic. 'A bit thick' is British slang for unreasonable.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something is a bit thick means it is more than one should be expected to put up with, unreasonable or over the top.

clue.text: Rabbi wearing possibly Persian cloth around neck

indicators.note: someone wearing something is wrapped in it, so the first piece goes inside the second

parts.note: a Persian is a breed of cat, so possibly signals an example
rav is a Hebrew title for a rabbi

explanation.surface: A rabbi is dressed in what may be a Persian scarf around his neck.
explanation.walkthrough: Persian looks like a rug or fabric; it is a breed of cat, and the cat ends up wrapped around the rabbi.
explanation.definitionFit: A cravat is a band of fabric worn tied at the throat, a forerunner of the necktie.

clue.text: Scots idiot's let out small sound of dissatisfaction

indicators.note: letting something out releases it, so that letter leaves the word

parts.note: sumph is a Scots word for a fool
S is the abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: A Scottish fool gives a little grunt of displeasure.
explanation.walkthrough: SUMPH loses its S to leave the answer; the 's of idiot's just stands for has.
explanation.definitionFit: Umph is an interjection, a grunt voicing doubt or displeasure, a spelling of humph.

clue.text: Gauge limit by resistance

parts.note: a mete is a boundary or limit
R is the physics symbol for resistance

explanation.surface: Measure a boundary in terms of electrical resistance.
explanation.definitionFit: A meter is an instrument for measuring, and a gauge is likewise a measuring device.

clue.text: Chatterer at Holyrood, even under pressure

indicators.note: in a down clue a piece placed under another is written below it, so it comes second

parts.note: P is the symbol for pressure
yet and even are interchangeable in phrases such as yet more

explanation.surface: A talkative Scottish politician keeps going even when pressed.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'under' puts the second piece below the first. Holyrood houses the Scottish Parliament, so it signals a Scots word.
explanation.definitionFit: Pyet is Scots for a magpie, a bird famous for its chattering call.

clue.text: More solid edging ought to feature on motorway

indicators.note: an edging runs around a border, so the first piece surrounds the second

parts.note: comparative of hard, firm or solid
should expresses obligation, as ought to does

explanation.surface: A road engineer says the motorway should have a firmer edge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Edging' looks like part of the road picture, but it is the container signal: the comparative wraps around the modal verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The hard shoulder is the paved strip along the edge of a British motorway, kept for emergencies.

clue.text: Unknown third-grade rating capturing stripped down rebel ship

indicators.note: stripping removes the outer layers, so the word loses its first and last letters
capturing something means holding it inside, so the pair encloses the stripped word

parts.note: x is the algebraic unknown
the word with its outer letters removed
a C is a third-grade mark after A and B

explanation.surface: An obscure low-ranking sailor seizes a mutineer's vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rating' suggests a sailor, matching 'ship', but here it is a grade mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A xebec is a small three-masted Mediterranean vessel, once favoured by corsairs.

clue.text: American weed which Darwin uses for bait

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a light-coloured tobacco grown in the US, weed being slang for tobacco
second meaning: Australian word for groundbait scattered to attract fish

explanation.surface: Charles Darwin is pictured using an American plant as bait.
explanation.walkthrough: Darwin is not the naturalist but the city in northern Australia, signalling an Australian word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a tobacco variety from Kentucky and, in Australia, chum thrown into water to draw fish.

clue.text: A talk outside Cambridge university about rarely seen particles

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: one word placed outside another surrounds it

parts.note: to natter is to chat idly

indicators.note: turning about means facing the other way, so the university's letters run backwards

parts.note: the Massachusetts Institute of Technology is in Cambridge, Massachusetts

explanation.surface: A lecture held outside a Cambridge university about particles rarely observed.
explanation.walkthrough: Cambridge suggests the English university, but it is the US one in Cambridge, Massachusetts.
explanation.definitionFit: Antimatter is made of antiparticles, which barely exist in nature and are seldom observed outside accelerators.

clue.text: Combined operations take in estimated attendance

indicators.note: placed in another word, these letters go inside it

parts.note: est is the abbreviation for estimated
CO is the abbreviation for Combined Operations
R, recipe, is the Latin for take used on prescriptions

explanation.surface: Military planners take in the estimated turnout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take in' reads as one phrase, but 'take' supplies the prescription abbreviation and 'in' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Escort can mean the act of accompanying someone, so being someone's escort is being in attendance on them.

clue.text: Salt endlessly unhappy thanks to ship's officer

indicators.note: without an end the word loses its final letter

parts.note: glum means downcast
ta is informal British for thanks
a mate is a merchant ship's deck officer

explanation.surface: An old salt is forever miserable because of the ship's officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Salt' invites an old sailor, which suits the ship; it is a chemical salt.
explanation.definitionFit: A glutamate is a salt or ester of glutamic acid, the best known being the flavour enhancer MSG.

clue.text: How nectar gatherers fly, totally draining empty lily

parts.note: to buzz a bottle is to drain it to the last drop

indicators.note: an empty word has had its inside removed, leaving just its outer letters

parts.note: only the first and last letters remain

explanation.surface: Bees fly about, sucking an empty lily completely dry.
explanation.walkthrough: BUZZ in the sense of finishing off a bottle completely is in Chambers; the bee picture makes it read as a noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Bees gather nectar and hum as they fly, so they move with a buzzing sound.

clue.text: Affected poultry could be so upset with little time left?

definitions.note: roupy means affected by roup, a bird disease

indicators.note: an upset thing is knocked into disorder, so its letters are rearranged
left in the sense of departed means those letters have gone from the word

parts.note: taken as written
little gives L as in the abbreviation l, time gives T

explanation.surface: Sick chickens might be so distressed if time were running out.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks what diseased poultry could be; the parse takes 'Affected' alone as the definition and rearranges the poultry once its L and T have gone.
explanation.definitionFit: Roup is an infectious respiratory disease of birds, so a fowl suffering from it is described as roupy.

clue.text: Large wild ox eating a shrub

indicators.note: something eating another takes it inside, so a letter goes into the pair

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for large
taken as written
the urus is the extinct wild ox, the aurochs

explanation.surface: A big wild ox munches on a bush.
explanation.definitionFit: Laurus is the genus of the bay laurel, an evergreen tree or bush, so a shrub.

clue.text: Impudence chap thus mostly confused with impedance

indicators.note: confused letters are muddled into a new order
mostly means all but a bit, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written; loses its last letter
Z is the physics symbol for impedance

explanation.surface: Someone muddles up impudence with impedance, as a cheeky chap might.
explanation.walkthrough: The near-identical words 'Impudence' and 'impedance' tempt the solver to treat them together; one is the definition, the other a physics symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: Chutzpah is Yiddish-derived for brazen nerve or audacity, which is impudence.

clue.text: Friend accepting Ian's denial about cause of weakness

indicators.note: accepting something means taking it in, so the denial goes inside the friend

parts.note: ami is French for friend
nae is Scots for no; Ian is a typical Scottish name
a is an abbreviation for about

explanation.surface: A friend accepts Ian's denial about what has made him weak.
explanation.walkthrough: Ian signals a Scot, so his denial is the Scots no; the friend wraps it after its first letter, and 'about' adds the final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Anaemia is a shortage of red blood cells or haemoglobin, which leaves a person tired and feeble.

clue.text: Relevant earlier question covers it

indicators.note: something that covers another wraps around it

parts.note: appose is an obsolete verb meaning to question or examine
taken as written

explanation.surface: A question asked earlier already deals with the relevant point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Earlier' marks an old word: APPOSE once meant to put questions to someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Apposite means well suited to the matter in hand, pertinent, which is to say relevant.

clue.text: Address for the old elevated part of the Hebrides

indicators.note: in a down clue raising a word means reading it upwards, from the bottom

parts.note: Harris is the southern part of the island of Lewis and Harris in the Outer Hebrides

explanation.surface: An address for elderly residents in a hilly part of the Hebrides.
explanation.walkthrough: Address looks like a postal location; it is a form of address, and 'the old' says it is no longer used.
explanation.definitionFit: Sirrah is an archaic contemptuous way of addressing a man or boy, a variant of sir.

clue.text: Sugar once boiled up in beer

indicators.note: placed in another word, these letters sit inside it

parts.note: ale is a kind of beer

indicators.note: in a down clue going up reads a word from the bottom

parts.note: sod is an old past tense of seethe, to boil

explanation.surface: Sugar was formerly boiled up in beer brewing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Once' marks the archaic past tense of seethe, which turns upward and goes inside the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: An aldose is a monosaccharide whose molecule contains an aldehyde group, glucose being one example.

clue.text: Gay Poulenc ballet males avoided

indicators.note: letters that are avoided are left out of the word

parts.note: Les Biches is a 1924 ballet scored by Francis Poulenc
hes are male people, as in he-goats

explanation.surface: A cheerful Poulenc ballet with no men in it.
explanation.walkthrough: Les Biches means the does or hinds; strip out the males and a word for lesbian is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Lesbic is an uncommon synonym for lesbian, and gay covers same-sex attraction in women too.

clue.text: Primarily Shah of Persia (historic Iran)

indicators.note: primarily means in the first place, so each word gives up its opening letter

parts.note: the first letters of the five words

explanation.surface: A note explaining that a shah was a ruler of Persia, the old name for Iran.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: the first letters spell the word and the clue describes it.
explanation.definitionFit: Sophi, or sophy, was a former title of the ruler of Persia under the Safavid dynasty.

clue.text: Rice dish is more Italian with input from Louisiana

indicators.note: input is something put into a thing, so these letters go inside

parts.note: più is Italian for more, familiar from musical directions
LA is the postal abbreviation for Louisiana

explanation.surface: A rice dish becomes more Italian with a contribution from Louisiana cooking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'More Italian' reads as a comparison; it means the Italian word for more.
explanation.definitionFit: Pilau is a spiced Eastern dish of rice cooked in stock, often with meat or vegetables.

clue.text: Bronchitis found in cattle hard by river

parts.note: H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard
the Usk is a river in south Wales

explanation.surface: Cattle grazing by a river have caught a bad cough.
explanation.definitionFit: Husk is a veterinary name for parasitic bronchitis in cattle, causing a dry husky cough.

clue.text: Icy period induced Indian tree to go over

indicators.note: going over means turning upside down, so the whole string is read backwards

parts.note: to lead someone to act is to induce them
the nim, or neem, is an Indian tree of the mahogany family

explanation.surface: A cold snap caused an Indian tree to topple.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mindel is the second of the Alpine glacial stages of the Pleistocene, an ice age.

clue.text: Ship's commercial officer, purser, a cog at sea

indicators.note: at sea means confused and adrift, so the letters are put into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A purser is just one small part of a ship's business at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: The purser looks like a second definition, as it is a ship's officer too, but it is only fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A supercargo is the person aboard a merchant ship who manages the cargo and its sale.

clue.text: Try breaking stone? Strewth!

indicators.note: something breaking into another gets inside it

parts.note: st is the abbreviation for the stone weight
to hear a case is to try it in court

explanation.surface: Someone attempts to smash a rock and swears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Try' reads as attempt; it is the judicial sense. 'Stone' is a British unit of weight, 14 pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: S'heart is an old oath from God's heart, like strewth, which comes from God's truth.

clue.text: Girl that is after golfer

indicators.note: coming after something means following it, so the phrase before this word is placed second

parts.note: Ernie Els is a South African golfer
i.e. is the abbreviation for id est, that is

explanation.surface: A girl is chasing a golfer.
explanation.definitionFit: Elsie is a girl's given name, so any female first name fits a clue of this kind.

clue.text: Mostly stony fell

indicators.note: mostly means all but a little, so the final letter goes

parts.note: stony, short for stony-broke, means penniless, as skint does

explanation.surface: A rocky hillside, as northern English fells mostly are.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fell' suggests a hill or a past tense; it is the noun for an animal's hide. Skint is British slang for broke.
explanation.definitionFit: A fell is an animal's hide or pelt, which is a skin.

clue.text: Excuse to stay up that could make one weary, nothing less

indicators.note: the letters could make a new word if rearranged, signalling a reshuffle
less means without, so that letter is removed

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Seeing in the New Year keeps people up late and leaves them tired.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a tidy self-description: staying up to midnight on 31 December is what makes one weary.
explanation.definitionFit: New Year's Eve is the one night people routinely stay up past midnight, so its arrival is an excuse.
